case_source: (From the judgment and Decree date 24-2-1966 passed by the Dacca High Court in S. A. No. 1917 of 1961).
full_judgment:
Kemaluddin Hossain, J. This is a Defendant's appeal by special leave arising out of a suit for recovery of possession of the suit land upon declaration of the plaintiffs title therein. The suit land is R.S. Plot No. 158 of mouza Madar Bari, Chittagong recorded in Khatian No. 234. Plaintiff says that the suit plot was recorded in raiyati right of Abdus Subhan. Plaintiff took, long lease of the land from the heirs of Subhan. This land is to the contiguous east of other lands of the plaintiff. They were wrongfully taken possession of by the defendants but the plaintiff succeeded in obtaining a decree for their eviction in Title Suit No. 5 of 1947. Out of spite for eviction, the defendants dispossessed the plaintiff by dismantling collie huts on the disputed lands 10 May, 1955. Hence the suit.

2. The appellant who is defendant No. 1 alone contested the suit. He denies plaintiff's title and the case of possession and dispossession. He challenges the correctness of the entry in the record of rights in the mine of Subhan He sets up his inherited tenancy right from his grandfather Ramzan Alternative he asserts that the suit is barred by adverse possession.

3. The learned Subordinate, Judge who tried the suit dismissed it, holding that the plaintiff failed to make out his title, and that the suit was barred by limitation, as the defendants were in adverse possession of the suit land for over 12 years.

4. On appeal by the plaintiff the first appellate Court found that the defendant's claim of title on the basis of Ext. B, Kabuliyat standing in the name of Ramzan did not subsist. He referred to two judgments, one in Title Suit No. 5 of 1941, and the other S.C.C. Suit No. 290 of 1941, Ext. 7(a) and 11. He also referred to Ext. F, written statement of Abdul Majid, father of defendant No. 1. Along with them, he considered Ext. 10, Khatian No. 234, relating to the suit land, and came to the conclusion that from these papers it was established that Ramzan's 5 years tenancy on the basis of Ext. was terminated by his superior landlord, Moifula Khatun, who in her turn settled the land with other tenants. The decisions of the aforesaid suits were binding on defendant No. 1 regarding this claim of title, As. regards plaintiff's title he differed with the, trial Court on the presumptive value of Khatian and treated it is evidence of title as well. He thereafter considered the oral and documentary evidence of both the plaintiff and defence on possession. He considered Ext. A to A4 Municipal demand register, Ext. C to C-7 the Municipal Tax receipts, Ext. G and G-l sale deeds, Ext. D and Ext. E filed by Defendant No. 1 and hold that they did not establish adverse possession of the defence on the suit land. He held so, after rejecting the second pleader commissioner's report. Earlier, a pleader commissioner's report had been rejected. The reason for rejecting the second report was that it was not prepared by surveying the land or with reference to the Municipal map. He disbelieved the defence witnesses but believed the plaintiff's witnesses, and found that the plaintiff succeeded in proving his dispossession in 1955 He hold that defendant No. 1 erected pucca and katcha structures on the land after dispossession of plaintiff. He also held that the plaintiff's suit was not barred by limitation. He reversed the decision of the Trial Court and decreed the suit.

5. The defendant No. 1 preferred a second appeal to the East Pakistan High Court and it was heard by a Division Bench. The High Court concurred with the First Appellate Court both as regards title and possession In favour of plaintiff and dismissed the appeal. The defendant No.1 appeal obtained leave from the Supreme Court of Pakistan to consider the following points.

i)Whether the plaintiff has failed to prove his title to the suit land and

ii)Whether oral and documentary evidence adduced by the defendant to prove his possession of the suit land for the statutory period, and which was accepted by the Subordinate Judge, did not receive due and full consideration in the appellate Courts.

6. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has appeared on behalf of defendant No. 1 appellant and Mr. M.H. Khandker for the plaintiff-Respondent. Learned Counsels of both sides have advanced lengthy, and learned arguments. We however, do not feel the necessity of adverting at length to them as we find that the question involved in this appeal should be disposed of with reference to points raised in the leave order.

<u>7.The points referred to in the leave order, though mentions question of title, and possession separately, yet in facts of the present case, the two questions are interdependent arid should be treated as such. It is to be remembered that the suit plot viz., R.S. 158 of Khatian No. 234 is part of the Kabuliyat land of Ramzan, grandfather of the appellant. We are to proceed with the questions of title and possession, keeping this basic fact in view. Both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 claim tenancy right in the land. They also claim possessory right over the land, defendant No. 1 claims expressly adverse possession, and plaintiff by implication, in tracing his title from Subhan. Plaintiff, however, came with the. story of possession followed by dispossession and is seeking eviction of defendants from the suit land. It is well settled that when a defendant is in possession, he could be evicted only by person having a better title than he. In such suit, plaintiff can only succeed by proving his better title over suit land. Has the plaintiff succeeded in doing so in the present case ?</u>

8. This question requires investigation and before we undertake it, it may be observed, that the concurrent findings of courts below cannot now be disturbed, regarding defendant No. 1's claim of tenancy right that it has failed. Evidence, documentary and oral, is ample to show that the Kabuliyat Ext. B of 1915 in favour of Ramzan, grandfather of Defendant No. 1 was terminated by the superior landlord, Moifula Khatun, who settled the land thereafter, with other tenants. In this view, a detailed discussion on defendant's title is not called for. But that does not automatically create title in favour of the plaintiff.

9. Plaintiff claims a derivative title from Subhan. According to him Subhan held the suit land in rayati right which was inherited by his heirs, two sons and wife, and they, by a patta, Ext. 4 dated 28-7-54, settled the land with him. Plaintiff in 1955 purchased the superior rayati right of his lessors, and thereby succeeded to the sixteen annas title of Subhan in the suit land. No doubt plaintiff.has produced the Patta Ext. 4, and the Kabla received from the heirs of Subhan one in 1954, and the other in 1955. The question is not the validity of the patta, but whether the lessors of the plaintiff had any transferable right. That again depends upon the fact whether they inherited any such transferable right from their predecessor, Subhan. Is there any evidence to show that Subhan held any tenancy right as claimed by the plaintiff ? The plaintiff except making his own bare assertion, and reliance on R.S. Khatian, Ext. 10, has adduced no evidence, oral or documentary. Plaintiff being a transferee from the heirs of Subhan, has not and cannot claim direct knowledge of the creation of tenancy in favour of Subhan. He could, however, lead evidence to prove the creation of tenancy. That he has not done. His case of title rests on the alleged presumption of correctness of settlement records.

10. The High Court has taken a view that although, an entry in the record of right would indicate the possessory right of the person whose name appears therein, but this also lends support to the claim of title made by the plaintiff. It seems to us, that this view of the High Court does not state the correct view of law on the presumption arising from the record of right. Both the learned counsel have on this point, cited a number of decisions. Apart from the cited decisions, there are a large number of authorities on this point, Some of them may be mentioned. Rani Harshamukhi Vs. Kshitindra, 47 C.W.N. 662, Anup Mahto Vs. Mita Dusadh 38 C.W.N. 365 (P.C.), Sri Nath Rai Vs. Pratap Udai Nath Sahi Deo, 28 C.W.N. 145 (P.C.), Pankajini Debi Vs. Suair Dutta 60 C.W.N. 793, Munnalal Vs. Mst. Kashibai 51 C.W.N. 175, Narendra Vs ( Rajendra 45 C.W.N. 654 ; Rai Kiran Chandra Roy Bahadur Vs. Srinath Chakrabarti 31 C.W.N. 135, Kumar Rai Vs. Baraboni Coal A.I.R. 1935 Calcutta 368, Jemarat Ali Vs. Rahman Sardar 17 D.L.R. Dacca 589, Pramatha Nath Vs. Kamir Mondal 17 D.L.R. (S.C.) 392.

11. Not all the cited authorities are. directly on the question before us, nor do we feel the necessity of referring to all of them in detail. From the cited decisions, we find that the preponderance of the judicial opinion is that the presumption of correctness arsing from the record of right under s. 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act raises a presumption of possession in favour of person whose name is recorded therein at the time of its final publication. No forward or backward presumption arises from correctness of record of right. For drawing backward presumption there must be some evidence. Forward presumption however is not available from the s. 103B of Bengal Tenancy Act, but a presumption of continuity may be drawn under s. 114 (d) of the Evidence Act. This forward presumption becomes weaker with the passage of time, and its probative value diminishes progressively with the lapse of time.

<u>12. Record of right is not a document of title. It does not create or extinguish title to land. At best, along with other evidence, it may support an evidence of title. By itself, it is not an evidence of title. The view of the High Court seems to have been overstated.</u>

13. We may now turn to the facts of the case. R.S. Khatian of the plot, Ext. 10, shows a tenancy was recorded in the name of Subhan under, Moifula Khatun. The record of right was published some time in 1927. Initial presumption of correctness of recording of possession of 1927 in favour of Subhan is there. Barring Khatian, the plaintiff has led no evidence on the creation of tide of Subhan. Plaintiff leading no evidence, either oral or documentary, cannot use the Khatian as evidence of title in favour of Subhan. The High Court was wrong in presuming title in favour of Subhan barely relying on Khatian. Bereft of this Khatian, there is no evidence of creation tenancy in favour of Subhan. The plaintiff has failed to prove that the heirs of Subhan acquired any transferable right to confer upon plaintiff by patta Ext. 4 Plaintiff has therefore valid to make out a valid title in his favour on the basis of Patta,

14. We have observed earlier that the questions of possession and title are interlinked in this case, and therefore the second question raised in the leave order is to be discussed along with the first question.

<u>15. With regard to possessory title, we find defendant No. 1 has expressly and the plaintiff impliedly claimed so. The First Appellate Court and the High Court no doubt have discussed the question of adverse possession of the defendant. They have also made a thorough discussion of the evidence as to dispossession of the plaintiff, and these findings cannot be assailed now. But then, unless the plaintiff can make out his title, he cannot recover possession, now that the Defendant-appellant is on the land. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has made strenuous effort in challenging the findings of the appellate Courts below, but a reference to the records reveals, that all relevant papers and oral evidence called by the appellant, have been thoroughly discussed the grievance of Mr. Chowdhury amounts to reconsideration of evidence afresh, a submission which is difficult to sustain.</u>

<u>16. Defendant No. 1’s claim both as regards title and adverse possession has failed; still then for the plaintiff to succeed, he has to make out a title in his favour. Though the plaintiff has failed on the acquisition of his title from Subhan's heir on the basis of Patta Ext. 4 yet prescriptive title of his predecessors may nonetheless subsist by continuous possession of Subhan and his heirs Plaintiff's registered patta Ext. 4 as a genuine document remains unchallenged, and so, if, he can show possessory title of his predecessors for the prescriptive period, he can still succeed in showing the acquisition of title in his favour. It appears, that this question bas not drawn the attention of either the First. Appellate Court or the High Court since they found title for plaintiff on the basis of patta But that finding having failed, this question assumes importance, and has now become decisive. It will be open to plaintiff to show the continuous possession of Subhan and his heirs, either direct or constructive on the Suit land for the prescriptive period before the grant of Patta in his favour. We feel that a determination of this question is necessary for complete adjudication of dispute between the parties. It is a mixed question of law and fact. We think therefore, the case should be remitted to the First appellate Court for decision of this narrow question; whether Subhan and his heirs were in possession direct or constructive at least from 1927, the year of publication of the Khatian till the Patta in 1954 was granted in favour of the plaintiff. Alternatively the plaintiff can show Subhan and/or his heirs were in possession for over the prescriptive period of 12 years prior to the grant of Patta on 28-7-54. Plaintiff, succeeding in establishing any of the alternatives, will be entitled to a decree for eviction on declaration of his title, as all other relevant questions have concurrently been held by the appellate Courts below in his favour. In this view of the matter, we refrain from making any observation on this question. The Court shall proceed to decide on the evidence already on record.</u>

17. In the result we allow the appeal in part. The decisions of the first appellate Court and the High Court regarding (a) the defence case of title and adverse possession have failed, and (b) the plaintiff has proved dispossession in May, 1955 are affirmed. The decisions of the said Courts below regarding the title of plaintiff are set aside and the appeal remitted back to the First Appellate Court to dispose of the question in the manner indicated above and in accordance with law. The First Appellate Court shall be at liberty to allow the parties to call such additional evidence on the question as it may deem fit.

In the circumstances of the case we make no order as to costs.

End.
